contributions.headingText: B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma (B-ALL/LBL) with KMT2A rearrangement is a neoplasm of lymphoblasts of B-cell lineage defined by the presence of a rearrangement between KMT2A and one of the numerous fusion partners.
2A70.Y & XH8GG0 Other B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma with recurrent genetic abnormalities & B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma with t(v;11q23); MLL-rearranged

B-ALL and B-LBL represent the same disease. B-ALL always involves the bone marrow and usually also involves the peripheral blood. Extramedullary involvement is common and is by definition the primary site of involvement in B-LBL. For details, see section B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma .

B-ALL/LBL with KMT2A rearrangement has clinical features similar to those of other clinical subtypes, but it more often has a high white blood cell count. CNS involvement is also common at presentation.

B-ALL with KMT2A rearrangement accounts for 70–80% of leukaemia cases in infants aged < 1 year {31283407}. It is less common in older children and then becomes increasingly common with age into adulthood.

The etiology is unknown. In infants and young children, the KMT2A rearrangement is typically acquired in utero {9391133; 10753857}. KMT2A breakpoints predominantly occur within an 8.3 kb region that includes multiple repeat sequences, DNase hypersensitivity sites, and targets for topoisomerase II cleavage, although the specific factors that affect breakage remain undefined {16797254}.

KMT2A (also known as MLL) is a histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methyltransferase. Rearrangements typically delete the methyltransferase domain and fuse KMT2A to a gene involved in transcription elongation {21118195}. This dysregulates both H3K4 and H3K79 methylation, resulting in upregulation of HOXA genes {15851025}. KMT2A rearrangement may be sufficient to drive leukaemogenesis, although leukaemias may harbour alterations of epigenetic modifiers or MAPK genes, including FLT3 {25730765}.

There are no unique morphological features.

Immunophenotype

Cases of B-ALL/LBL with KMT2A rearrangements, especially t(4;11), typically have a CD19+, CD10−, CD24− immunophenotype and are often positive for the myeloid markers CD15 and CD65s, as well as the neural/glial antigen CSPG4 (NG2) {12094248; 6958337; 12200682; 17851550}. TdT negativity, which is uncommon in B-ALL/LBL overall, is also relatively frequent in B-ALL/LB with KMT2A rearrangement {34148065}.

Differential diagnosis

In some cases, it may be possible to recognize distinct lymphoblastic and monoblastic populations, a finding that can be confirmed by immunophenotyping; at diagnosis, such cases should be considered B/myeloid mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia. B-ALL/LBL with KMT2A rearrangement may undergo a lineage switch after either conventional therapy or anti-CD19–directed therapy {22685031; 33749383}.

More than 90 different gene partners for KMT2A have been identified across all leukaemia types {28701730}. The seven most common fusion partners account for > 90% of cases (see #30679Table 4.11).

B-ALL/LBL with KMT2A rearrangement is suspected by translocations/inversions at 11q23 in chromosome studies but requires verification by FISH, RT-PCR, or next-generation sequencing evaluation. KMT2A rearrangements can be cryptic by karyotype and/or FISH studies and require next-generation sequencing evaluation, which exemplifies the variable and complex genomics that can occur with KMT2A, particularly in infant/paediatric leukaemia {27282883; 32196814}.

Essential: meets the diagnostic criteria for B-ALL/LBL (see section B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma); immunophenotyping by FACS and/or immunohistochemistry to explore a frequently present immunophenotype (negative for CD10, CD24, and TdT; positive for myeloid markers CD15, CD65s, and NG2); demonstration of KMT2A rearrangement by FISH and/or RT-PCR and/or next-generation sequencing analysis.

Desirable: identification of KMT2A rearrangement partner.

B-ALL/LBL with KMT2A rearrangement generally has a poor prognosis compared with other genetic types across age groups. The relative risk associated with different KMT2A partners continues to be a topic of investigation {34525185; 31283407; 12682627}.
